Portable Pocket WOWOTO Projector Android Mini Smart LED DLP Projector I was actually really shocked at how great this little portable speaker is. My cell phone found it in seconds, and in less than a minute I was listening to music from my cell phone, only out of this little speaker, it actually sounded great. In fact, the bass was so effective out of this thing that some of my favorite songs made it dance around the table.

I love that it is so much louder than the music I get out of my cell phone, and I also love that I can listen to hip-hop and rap and enjoy actual bass, which usually doesn't come through for my cell phone speaker at all.

You can actually control the music from your cell phone from the speaker itself. It has a pause/play button, forward and back, and volume controls. It also has a speakerphone control, in case you wanted to have a quick conversation from the speaker itself. I would not personally want to use the speaker as a speakerphone, but it is nice to have the option in a pinch.

The one thing I didn't care for is that when you tap the volume button and it hits its maximum, it beeps at you to let you know that it won't go any louder. It's a pretty annoying sound, and in my view they could just have left that feature out. I'm sure I would figure it out soon enough that it wouldn't go any louder.

Overall, I was really surprised at the quality, ease of setup, and range of sound from this cute little speaker. I'm delighted to own it, and anticipate it getting a lot of use over the coming months and years.
text_fidelity_b: Portable Pocket WOWOTO Projector Android Mini Smart LED DLP Projector

NETGEAR WiFi Mesh Range Extender EX7500 - Coverage up to 2300 sq.ft. and 45 devices with AC2200 Tri-Band Wireless Signal Booster & Repeater (up to 2200Mbps speed), plus Mesh Smart Roaming I bought this extender at the same time that I bought an Orbi with one satellite. I figured that even if the Orbi did not work out, the EX7500 would be helpful with my then-current setup (four Apple wifi routers that could barely cover my home).

The jury is still out on the Orbi system, as I have had to reset it a couple of times already, and it does not play all that well with all of my smart devices. BUT the EX7500 is a trouper. I have not had to do one thing to this extender beyond plugging it in and setting it up once. Setup itself was easy and took under five minutes. Adding it to the Orbi network increased my speed in the farthest ranges of my house by a good 50-75 Mbps.

I've had other extenders that, for example, gave me duplicate IP address errors and/or constantly snatched my wifi connection. My Apple extenders let excluded MAC addresses onto my network unless I duplicated those settings for each extender. This one runs completely invisibly. It's probably the most troublefree extender I've ever owned. Seriously. It is wicked expensive, but it is the one piece of networking equipment I currently own, including my Apple setup and the Orbi, that I can definitely say that I am keeping.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR WiFi Mesh Range Extender EX7500 - Coverage up to 2300 sq.ft. and 45 devices with AC2200 Tri-Band Wireless Signal Booster & Repeater (up to 2200Mbps speed), plus Mesh Smart Roaming

No custom settings on the software.

I performed the basic troubleshooting; uninstalled and reinstalled the software, unplugged the cam several times, checked my system updates, and restarted my system a couple of times. Zero. Zip. Zilch. Nada. Nothing worked. Then I tried customer support on Anker's website.

I was 1st in line for support. WooHoo! Nope, false hopes. I sat in the chat window for 15 minutes. Nothing. I reloaded chat, was 1st again. Waiting 15 mins. Nothing. Wow, Anker is known for their customer service but they really bombed this time.

Others have experienced these cam issues but it's not many. Maybe I got a dud? Anything's possible, but the lack of customer service is inexcusable. Cam Returned. Going back to Logitech. Sorry Anker, maybe you should stick with chargers.

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Tablet Mouse for Android 3.1+ You just cannot go wrong with a Logitech mouse, and this one is no exception. Sleek and sexy, well-designed and reliable, this tablet mouse for Android 3.1+ is a joy to hold. I love the color, too. It reminds me of my beloved old teal Logitech corded mouse that wouldn't work with the newer computers. This is a notebook-sized mouse, which is the size I prefer. It is not as tiny as some of the little mice out there, though. Not too big, not to small; just right.

Logitech stresses that this is an Android mouse and that it's not going to work properly with anything older than Android 3.1. It's even in the product title, so it's obvious that the OS is important, but I'm sure there will be people out there who will think it's going to work with earlier versions of Android. I wouldn't chance it. Some other reviewers have reported successfully pairing this mouse with non-Android systems, but I haven't been able to. It did happily meet and greet a friend's tablet PC, however.

Note that, unlike some Logitech mice, this mouse does NOT have a dongle, so you must have a bluetooth-enabled machine to use it. I tried it with a generic bluetooth dongle on my Windows Vista laptop, and I couldn't get it to work. That's not the mouse's fault. One good thing about it is that you can use it with a bluetooth keyboard; if I were going to get one, I'd go with Logitech's keyboard so I know they'll play nice.

I haven't had the opportunity to run down the batteries of this mouse, but if this one is like the other Logitech mice I own, the batteries last a long, long time--unlike competitors' mice, which seem to chew up and spit out batteries every few weeks. You can turn the mouse off, of course, but the sleep function also conserves batteries. Very nice.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Tablet Mouse for Android 3.1+

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech HD Laptop Webcam C615 with Fold-and-Go Design, 360-Degree Swivel, 1080p Camera I was able to compare this directly to the Logitech C525. They both have the same "fold and go" design, but I was surprised that the C615 is a bit heavier, and I think a millimeter or two thicker. It's well worth it, because the optics are better, and not just better because the resolution is higher - the quality is simply better.

The tripod mount is a nice addition over the C525, adding versitility in positioning. I suppose this would also help you set it up as a hidden camera, or just keep a pile of dirty laundry out of the view mounting on your laptop might otherwise provide.

As others have mentioned, there is a USB extender, which is nice. However, I would much rather have seen a long (or even a very short) cable provided with a microUSB connection to the actual device, allowing the device to become truly portable, rather than having a nice foldable, portable device with a cumbersome cord permanently attached. The user could then use the same cable they charge their smartphone with. Thankfully, the cord is placed in such a way that allows for full 360 degree rotation.

Note that although you can record 1080 videos with this device, you can only chat in 720 - another consideration if you just want this for Skype or another chat program.

Overall, this is the most appealing webcam on the market to me. The most important thing is that it can be tossed in a bag or pocket with other electronics without having to worry about the lens getting scratched.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech HD Laptop Webcam C615 with Fold-and-Go Design, 360-Degree Swivel, 1080p Camera

It is amazingly small and compact, not much bigger than my cell phone. It is an attractive blue color. It is good value for the money in terms of a full 4TB of storage. The packaging is very easy to open--no clamshell plastic.

What I had big problems with, and which took hours of struggle to figure out and try to resolve:

I currently have two older EHD, and when I hooked this EHD to the same USB hub as them, my desktop PC would not allow me to eject this EHD. Worse, Windows would shut down, and I had to turn off the PC manually.

Also be aware that if you, as I do, have an older computer with several outdated USB 2.0 ports, or a USB hub that is 2.0, this EHD won't work as well with them as with USB 3.0. If you need to use an extension data cable, be sure as well to buy 3.0.

text_fidelity_a: Panasonic LUMIX FZ1000 II 20.1MP Digital Camera, 16x 25-400mm LEICA DC Lens, 4K Video, Optical Image Stabilizer and 3.0-inch Display – Point and Shoot Camera - DC-FZ1000M2 (Black) This is a really nice superzoom camera for those who like to (or have to) travel light. I normally use a 7D Mk ii with various telephoto prime and telephoto zooms for wildlife photography and 5D Mk iv with wide angle prime and zooms for landscape shots. I recently had to go on a trip where it was impossible to bring any of my DSLR kits due to space and weight limitations. I was able get a super deal on a Panasonic FZ-1000 (I guess this is quite an older model at this time). I was somewhat skeptical about the specs at first, but the Leica lens and the 1" sensor performed really well on my test shots, so I decided to take the FZ-1000 as my camera for the trip. The results were surprisingly good. The camera has quick and intuitive user interface, good set of manual controls and several programmable function buttons, so it is relatively easy to learn and set it up to one's preferences. The AF system certainly exceeded my expectations. It did an excellent job of picking subjects behind branches/partial foliage. The success rate for birds in flight was quite good, not nearly as fast or accurate as a 7D Mk ii with EF 400 f/5.6L, but good enough for all practical purposes. Exposure both in scene mode and spot mode (a somewhat large spot) was good. Battery life was also very good. I was getting more than 600 shots per charge using the optical viewfinder and no flash. I did not try the 4K video feature yet, but the 1080p video quality was also very good. The whole package is as big as a low-end DSLR with a kit lens, but gives you 25mm-400mm effective focal range, a relatively fast lens (f/4.0 even at 400mm) plenty of manual control, and a very good AE/AF system. Highly recommended for travel when there is space/weight limitations.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic LUMIX FZ1000 II 20.1MP Digital Camera, 16x 25-400mm LEICA DC Lens, 4K Video, Optical Image Stabilizer and 3.0-inch Display – Point and Shoot Camera - DC-FZ1000M2 (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Washable Wired Keyboard K310 I often eat at my desk, which is not the greatest thing. Croissant flakes, bits of cheese and even rice grains often find their way into the crevices of my standard keyboard at work. It gets really disgusting. A few times crumbs got stuck inside the keys and stopped them from working properly. I've used compressed air cans and mini vaccuums but they don't do that great a job. I often end up having to flip the thing over and give it a shake. In addition, I remove all the keys and use a Q-tip to wipe up dust and dirt that get encrusted in these tiny spaces, which is time-consuming.

So you can tell I was relieved to get this washable keyboard. This thing is made for the Oscar Madisons of the world (like me). While you can't use it underwater while scuba diving (the instructions say you shouldn't submerge it in more than 11" of water, and no more than 5 minutes at that), being able to do a wash and rinse (as if it were a dinner plate) is more than enough to get most dirt and crumbs out.

I also like the fact that there is no additional software to install - just plug into the standard USB port, wait a few minutes until your computer recognizes the hardware, and then you're off. The keyboard is about the same size as other computer keyboards, except that the keys feel more like ones you'd find on a laptop. They are round and smooth and make me feel I'm pushing buttons. Because they lay flatter on the surface of the keyboard, you get a softer sound when you type as opposed to the hardier tapping of regular keyboards.

It took me awhile to get used to the feel. The buttons lack the slightly concave ridges that keep your fingers nestled so my fingers felt slippery on them, but not enough to have a problem.

Despite these reservations, however, I think this is a well-made product that is very practical, especially for people like me, who'd rather write than clean. Now all I need is a washable mouse!
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Washable Wired Keyboard K310

Konnek Stein True Wireless Earbuds, Bluetooth 5.1 Active Noise Cancelling Headphones, Sliding Design Charging Case 500mAh, IPX4 Waterproof, Deep Bass Built-in Mic Call for Business & Sports - Black The KONNEK STEIN True Wireless Earbuds are a decent set of wireless earbuds. The sound quality is good, I’ve been using them with music and streaming shows, and I haven’t been disappointed with the sound quality.

I’m not as pleased with the short battery life, touch controls, and lack of audio cues.

I get about 2-3 hours of playback per charge. It’s rare for me to battery drain earbuds, but with this pair, I hear the low battery chime every time I use them.

The touch controls and lack of audio cues go together. The touch controls are super easy to activate on accident. More than once I’ve taken the earbuds out only to find I hit Play while doing so, and they kept playing music. I also activate random controls when adjusting the earbuds in my ears … and I don’t always know what I’ve done. Did I turn ANC on or off? The audio cues are just beeps, not an announcement like “ANC on/ANC off.”

I like the design of the case. It has a sliding top, so you can actually clean the entire area where the earbuds sit. When you put the earbuds inside the case, a light flashes to show their battery level. The case charges wirelessly or via USB-C. There’s only one LED light on the outside of the case, it’s easy to miss when you’re trying to see if the case is charging or not.
text_fidelity_b: Konnek Stein True Wireless Earbuds, Bluetooth 5.1 Active Noise Cancelling Headphones, Sliding Design Charging Case 500mAh, IPX4 Waterproof, Deep Bass Built-in Mic Call for Business & Sports - Black

LeadsaiL Wireless Computer Mouse, 2.4G Portable Slim Cordless Mouse Less Noise for Laptop Optical Mouse with 4 Buttons, AA Battery Used, USB Mouse for Laptop, Desktop, MacBook Great shape, very much like the classic and ubiquitous Logitech. I like that the pairing device is on-board. Lightweight and simple, a mouse is important for me if needing to get serious work done, especially anything with CAD or Visio.

The big question you need to ask yourself is, do you want a Bluetooth version or one like this that has its own receiver. It seems to me that if you always use this with the same computer and you have Bluetooth built in to the computer, then you probably want Bluetooth. Conversely, if you want this to use with multiple computers and/or you don't have Bluetooth built in to any one of the computers you will use the mouse with, then you'd want something like this. This is because pairing is easier in a case such as this, and drivers usually aren't an issue. Bluetooth usually isn't an issue either, but it might get irritating with frequent changing of machines. At least that is my experience.

Does not come with a carry bag, surprisingly. Mouse roller also functions as a button, as it should. It has an on/off switch on the back, which is nice for saving battery life and being able to leave this hooked up to a permanent install (although with a permanent desk setup, I personally stick with wired).

Apple 12.9-inch iPad Pro Wi-Fi + Cellular - 12.9" Tablet - 256 GB - 3G/4G - GOLD There is so much talk about the declining sales of iPad. So much so, the discussion might influence a potential buyer to pause before buying or not buy at all, and instead buy a competing tablet or laptop. I think the key to making a decision to buy the iPad Pro lies in a wallpaper Apple provided with the very first version of iPad. It was a licensed photograph of Pyramid Lake by Robert Misrach. The exposure, made at night, appears to be in daylight. The clue that it was a night time photograph are the star trails that resulted from the long exposure. The lake surface appears as smooth as a mirror. The mirror surface of the lake in this photograph enables the viewer to immerse himself or herself in the device, making it a perfect fulfillment of whatever there desires might be "for iPad". The iPad is a perfect "evocative object", evoking whatever feelings and intentions the iPad user brings to it. That is why the iPad is so undefinable and uncategorizable. It is is whatever ever we want it to be.....and with iPad Pro Apple reaches again for that elusive quality.

After 7 days with the new Apple iPad Pro I am happy that I followed my hunch that the iPad Pro would be better for me than a laptop for a mobile multi-purpose device. I am very pleased how the slide over multitasking works. Bigger is better whether using multi-tasking features live slide over and picture-in-picture. The user does not get poorly sized Windows for both applications. For example if your browser is open in one window, and photos is open in a second, but applications are scaled to size in each window.

I purchased the 32MB version because I tend to use iCloud to store photos, music, documents. I only need local storage for IOS apps and the few documents I need.

I purchased a black rear cover, and a contrasting white front cover. The only accessory I use so far is the Apple Pencil for drawing in Paper by 53 and Apple Notes ( to take notes in my University classes ). I use the iPad Pro almost exclusively landscape or horizontal, the only iPad that can be used in portrait is the Mini. At the time I purchased the iPad Pro the wait times for shipment of the Apple Pencil was 4-5 weeks. However, I was able to find one locally at my University Bookstore. I am concentrating on using the Apple Pencil at the moment, using just the on-screen keyboard. I have an open mind about buying the iPad Pro keyboard in the future. However, the iPad is all about creating art through use of touch and the pencil right now. I don't want it to be a laptop. I want it to be a "blank sheet of paper".

The audio produced by the 4 speakers produce a very pleasing music listening experience without headphones.

One final note: it appears the iPad Pro includes technology that can be used in the future today's blog post in Daring Fireball notes that the Lightning connector includes support for USB 3.0, a much faster transfer speeds. It will be interesting to see what applications take advantage of that speed next year.

Microsoft Wired Keyboard 600 (Black). Wired Keyboard for Gaming Experience. USB Connectivity. Spill Resistant Design. This is a very basic keyboard, but it gets nearly everything right. The layout adheres to the QUERTY convention, it has illuminated indicators for caps and num lock, it has a numeric keypad, and basic multimedia controls (play/pause and volume). It covers all of the bases for a basic keyboard.

The key feel is nice. It's quiet, and the keys are comfortable to press. The function keys are smaller than the other keys to save on space but work just fine. The attached USB cord is nice and long (about 6 foot). The overall build quality feels decently solid for the price point. It auto installed on Win 10 without a hitch.

Misses are minor. It lacks a sleep button. It has a calculator button instead that, for me, is far less useful than a sleep button. It also lacks non-slip pads on the base. There are two legs that can be used to prop up the keyboard, but the keyboard is so light that it's easy to shift the position of it in use. I solved it with some stick-on non-slip material.

I've always used Microsoft keyboards and have yet to have one fail on me. There are other basic keyboards that are a dollar or two less expensive than this, but considering this is less than $11, I'd rate the overall value as very good. If you're looking for a basic, everyday keyboard and don't need/want anything fancy, this will fit the bill well and do so at a great price. Five stars.
text_fidelity_b: Microsoft Wired Keyboard 600 (Black). Wired Keyboard for Gaming Experience. USB Connectivity. Spill Resistant Design.

text_fidelity_a:
GRADO SR80e Prestige Series Headphones The first thing I noted when I listened to these much-celebrated headphones (at least the Prestige line at any rate) is how incredibly exaggerated the low-end is. While getting that kind of bass response from a headphone driver is impressive, showing it off at the expense of fidelity is not something I particularly care for. When using these on a device where a DAC is involved, such as an iPad, I have to use the 'bass reducer' EQ profile on the device or the sound will otherwise will be muddy with distortion. I am sure this has a lot to do with the dinky amplifier inside the iPad being unable to fully drive the the whopping 32 ohms of resistance the SR80e pushes back with. As a rule, underpowered amplifiers are what ruin the drivers inside speakers or headphones so when you hear distortion it means your amplifier is underpowered when matched with the driver and you need to change one of those two things. When you hear distortion from a crappy amplifier that's the sound of your speakers being slowly ruined so you really want to avoid this. (I always have a sad chuckle when some punk is walking the streets with ghetto blaster at maximum volume and the sound is atrocious- little does he know that what people are annoyed by is not the volume, but the distortion! Plus he's ruining his equipment.)

Using the SR80e with a mobile device is a case where an external headphone amplifier would be highly desirable, if not required, so this is a bit of an ask. I have not had a lot of success with the in-line amplifiers designed to run off of the device's power (specifically the Lightning-DAC-and-amplifier combos that you can buy to replace the dongle that Apple ships with their new iPhones) where I played recordings which have very high amplitude levels. For these recordings, the distortion is intolerable even though records at a nominal recording level sound great. The lack of gain control is a real problem with these gadgets- something that is de-facto on any headphone amp that you don't put in your pocket. Therefore, you'll be reduced to using headphones like these at home or work, which is where I use mine.

The fact that you have to significantly alter the EQ profile of your audio player to even have these cans reproduce a sound that is remotely like the original recording violates "high fidelity" by definition. Compare this to a sound engineer style headphone set like Sony MDR Pros which are designed to reproduce the source signal as accurately as possible. This is what "high fidelity" actually means. Some people may not like this and will end up using some artificial bass boost on their device to compensate, which the MDRs will gladly deliver. Most people who listen to popular music are generally accustomed to excessive bass. If that is the sort of listener that you are, then these headphones are for you because once you get the SR80s tuned properly, the sound these cans deliver is very impressive. Very. Impressive.

Unfortunately, when using an IOS device, playing this profile with even high end earbuds like the UE Triple Fis, the sound will be tinny, so toggling between the two modes by way of a shortcut would be a nice bonus, but as it stands I have to go deep into the preferences to change this setting. Therefore, I would only recommend these headphones if you intend to use them in a stationary location. Since these are very high resistance earphones (even higher than most loudspeakers for that matter) you really ought to get an headphone amplifier if you want these to shine.

One other issue is with the minimalist foam cup pads. While they are comfy, they do not block sound in or out whatsoever, so if you use them in a noisy office you will be annoyed at how loud you have to play these to drown out ambient noise. Also, your workmates will probably be annoyed by the bleed through. I ended up getting a different cup pad kit which is marginally better, but it changes the fit somewhat so it takes a little fiddling to get them to sit on your skull around your ears evenly. Otherwise, the headphones are incredibly comfortable as they are very lightweight, which is surprising considering the size of the driver. Grado has found the sweet spot between having a massive (and heavy) drive coil magnet and being featherweight, even if I might take issue with their choices about fidelity reproduction.

Tl;DR: If you really like your sound overcharged with bass, these are the headphones for you. Otherwise, if you are looking for a quality but moderately priced pair of headphones, you might be better off with a more reference-style set like the Sony MDRs.
text_fidelity_b: GRADO SR80e Prestige Series Headphones

Jabra STONE Bluetooth Headset with Extreme-Noise Blocking (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I think this is a good electronic gadget. Actually, it made me upgrade my phone to one that uses Bluetooth. I was still using a cell phone that only lets you receive and make calls, and play a few games so I guess it was time to move forward technically speaking.

The sound is clear, I had my daughter answer the phone at home while I was driving and it worked marvelously. She could easily understand me and vice-versa. After I got home I put my cell phone on the kitchen table after calling my land-line and I walked outside of the house with the Jabra Stone only. I was surprised that I was still able to talk to my daughter from almost 100 feet away from my cell phone. As I walked down the driveway and into the street it finally lost connection. But, I know that at least within a few feet I don't need to always have my cell phone right with me.

The Jabra Stone worked just like the directions said it would but I still kept messing it up during the learning curve. I wish it was a little more secure around my ear and for those who like to tuck their long hair behind their ears (me) it's difficult to do that with the earpiece on. And I have to remember to untuck my hair before putting it on or it will not go on. But once you get the hair problem solved it's well hidden - I don't think anyone can see it while I wear it. Also, it only works for the right ear, at least as far as I can tell so I don't know if it can be modified some way to hook on the left ear. I tried to fit onto my left ear but couldn't figure out a way to do so. So, if you are deaf in your right ear I would check to make sure it could be changed somehow to fit the left ear.

It's small, convenient and functional. So much easier than trying to drive and hold a phone at the same time, but I rarely drive and yak on the phone anyway since it's so dangerous. I don't want to be distracted from driving. But when out shopping or doing something else on foot and I'm expecting an important call it's great to have my hands free to continue shopping as I yak.

The reason for 4 stars instead of 5 - kind of loose on my ear, and the charger doesn't hold a charge for very long. It's frequently plugged into the wall re-charging. But it's great that you can hook the charger to your shirt pocket (men will like that) so you can continue to receive calls all day long.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra STONE Bluetooth Headset with Extreme-Noise Blocking (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a: TOMSHOO Portable Folding Windproof Wood Burning Stove Compact Stainless Steel Alcohol Stove Outdoor Camping Hiking Backpacking Picnic BBQ As all Amazon deliveries have been for at least a month, since they dropped the USPS, this one was late.  Unacceptable performance.  This is a great twig stove.  Collapses into a small package and it use it burns hot and clean. Very efficient, leaving virtually no ash or charcoal.  I've had other similar stoves, including an Ohuhu (?) brand.  That one was nicer in one respect, it had no slotted cross pieces which this one has to space the pot above the flames.  In the dark, or when moving and setting up the stove several times a day these little bits could easily be lost.  the other stove had fold-out bits to support the pot. So, nothing to lose, but the folding part was slightly weak and could be broken or mis aligned.  So it's all about equal i suppose.  Anyway, filled with small fuel and started from the top this stove is very efficient and boils water at least as fast as any little gas stove i've used.  The "bio-fuel" system of heating the ignition air really does burn nearly smoke free.  If the stove is smoking you may have over-fed it or have fuel sticking above the hot-air feed holes.  I got at least 400 burns out of my last little SS twig stove and i never took any great care to be nice to it...and eventually wore it out.  If i get 400 burns out of this one i'll be a happy guy.  In short, if you are looking for a twig stove to burn what you find on the trail or around camp give this one a try, you'll probably like it.

Motorola CommandOne Bluetooth Headset - Retail Packaging One of the most important attributes for a headset is comfort. I've tried a few over the years, but always have found them to be a pain (literally!) if they are worn for more than 20 minutes or so. I'm very happy to report that the Moto is a dream when it comes to comfort - had it on for a three+ hour drive, and didn't even know it was there. Plus, it didn't cause a problem with my glasses, unlike other models I've tried.

Set up was very straightforward - basically just follow the prompts and it works. I didn't try out the text-to-voice feature but it sounds interesting. Not really something I would use since I don't text much at all, but if you're text-heavy, that feature would certainly be of value.

Audio quality was excellent. Had no problems hearing callers even with music playing in the car. Range was also very good.

My complaints are two-fold. First a minor one - this comes packed in what I would consider to be wasteful packaging. Looks impressive in a clear, thick plastic box, but the amount of materials used for packing is unnecessary. I did not, however, deduct anything from its rating due to that.

What did cause a loss of one star was the mic pickup. In a quiet environment it was fine. But, in a noisy environment (such as outside, in a crowded restaurant or with moderate-level music playing in the car), it picks up so much background noise that people had problems hearing me. To ensure this was actually the case, I loaned it to a friend and had him call me so I could hear for myself. It seems that the mic is either way too sensitive or not sufficiently directional - it truly is hard to hear the person's voice when they are using the headset should they be in anything other than a pretty quiet environment..

But, that aside, this is the best headset I've used to date. Especially recommended if you have had comfort issues with other headsets or are a glasses wearer.
text_fidelity_b: Motorola CommandOne Bluetooth Headset - Retail Packaging

Munitio SV Mobile Performance Earphones with 3 Button Mic Control, Bronze Lower and mid end earphones have generally been lacking in both quality and performance. Given my propensity to misplace them, I have been reluctant to invest in more expensive versions. But with increased reliance on mobile devices, it was most definitely time to upgrade.

My familiarity with Munitio was more from their urban chic style complete with bullet motif, Kevlar coated cord, "tactical" carrying case and "hollow point" ear cups. At the risk of looking more Duck dynasty than cool, I was eager to try them.

Designed for use with Apple devices, the phones come securely packaged in a black carrying case. The look is sleek and modern and the bronze color is appealing. These are also available in black and gray. There are three sets of ear cups in different sizes. They were comfortable and shut out outside noise. The cord is flat and tangle free with a heft that promises durability. The 3 button mic control is located on the upper left hand side of the earphone cable. I really couldn't see the buttons but quickly mastered them by touch. They provide full functionality for calls and music on iPods, iPods and iPhones and just music for other mp3 players and Android devices.

I encountered no difficulties in making or taking calls. I could hear the other party and they could hear me without difficulty. The mic is positioned close enough to the mouth and is sufficiently sensitive that I didn't have to scream or repeat things. I made calls from a fairly busy coffee shop and a mall and ambient noise did not impair the call quality.

I tried these earphones with my IPod and a cheap mp3 player of dubious lineage. The sound was clear, strong and enjoyable. I did not find the bass overwhelming and was generally pleased with the performance.

Bottom line, I liked these earphones. The case and the trio of ear cups are thoughtful touches. Although light, there is a sense of substance and quality. The controls are intuitive and easy to use. There is a two year limited warranty. Serving up generous doses of comfort, convenience and performance, these ear phones are right on target.
text_fidelity_b: Munitio SV Mobile Performance Earphones with 3 Button Mic Control, Bronze

text_fidelity_a:
Kodak PlayFull ZE2 Waterproof Video Camera with 2x Optical Zoom and 2-Inch LCD Screen (Black) I made absolutely sure everything was closed before putting it into water, not that one could have much faith in the mechanisms keeping it closed, as they are easy to accidentally open. I put it in the water gently, and only a foot or so, to film some stingrays and fish; this recording went fine. Later that day, I wanted to photograph a tiny little crab. I took one picture from above the water, and one from below. I noticed this time, when I put the camera underwater, that bubbles started to come out the top. I immediately took it out and noticed the screen starting to fog up with condensation and moisture, the first very bad sign. I double checked everything was still closed, and it was. No part of it had been opened. I put it back in, hoping for the best. After coming back to the sand (never having done more than a few feet underwater), I tried to turn it on to get some video. It would not turn on. I checked again, and nothing appeared to be open. I then dried the exterior and opened it, only to discover there was water on the inside. I immediately removed the SD card, in hopes of salvaging it, but the camera was (is) completely dead.

Two days later, there is corrosion forming on the inside from the water, but at least I salvaged the content on the SD card. The results? Video quality is fine above and below water. Photo quality is a mess. Absolutely the worst pics imaginable.
I am so glad I didn't have to pay for this product; I would have been furious it didn't even last a day in the ocean.

I expected more, since I had previously purchased a "Kodak EasyShare Sport C123 12 MP Waterproof Digital Camera", which has been great! That product never failed after much abuse and takes decent picture and video. I'm not sure what happened here, but buyer beware! Try the EasyShare Sport instead.

I'll post some pictures and, if it lets me, some video too. I hope you all find this helpful!

UPDATE: I can't post video (sorry)
Also, I looked at some other reviews that mentioned water getting in while at the pool or in other non-salinated water. Bear in mind that many electronics can survive water immersion if it is fresh water (as opposed to salt water). Many of these reviewers gave the camera more than one star because it was able to work again, but bear in mind this will NOT hold true it Salt water enters the device. Please consider this.
text_fidelity_b: Kodak PlayFull ZE2 Waterproof Video Camera with 2x Optical Zoom and 2-Inch LCD Screen (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
GAOMON PD1560 15.6 Inches 8192 Levels Pen Display with Arm Stand 1920 x 1080 HD IPS Screen Drawing Tablet with 10 Shortcut Keys TL:DR - if you want a good tablet from a brand that cares about it's customers/users AND has good drivers/software in a 16" screen you can't go wrong with this device. Huion Kamvas Pros are good and all, but I've heard too many issues compared to this device with virtually none. Especially considering the total cost is around 350 - 375.

It's not perfect and pickier users like me may not like some of the workarounds, but for a first art tablet that is basically what I'd consider the best package and/or intro into digital art you can't go wrong.

The GAOMON PD1560 really surprised me with it's performance to price ratio. The device itself is light weight and comes with what I would dub as a starter bundle of accessories. Tablet, Stand, Glove, Nibs, Carrying case, etc. The line quality is also really amazing and when running my tests didn't notice any abnormal line wobble if any at all. Brad Coblow does a good review of it. Contratry to his review the quality isn't bad at all. If you've handled a computer monitor this tablet feels like it more or less. Drivers weren't an issue and the hot keys were fantastic.

The pen kept a great charge and felt nice to use along with the included artist glove (I got only a single two finger one). Drawing without the screen protector was a little squeaky at times, but had no issue in CS6 and CSP. The tablet stays nearly completely when you adjust the brightness/backlit to sub 65 degrees F. Luckily it doesn't change the looks all that much. There is a bit of parallax and calibration can take some time to get completely right but pen accuracy is top notch.

Screen quality is good and the cables are pretty rigid so no worries there. They actually connect by recessing into a slot rather than on the edge of the device.

Lastly is customer service. I really enjoyed GAOMON's customer service which I wish more companies would do.

There are a few caveats though. To get the pen the most accurate no matter where you point on the screen you need to understand where you touch the dot when calibrating. Next you need to hold the pen in the exact same orientation and way when you draw. That means holding the pen the exact same way with little deviation of that angle to get things to line up as well as say an iPad Pro. If you don't the distance when you calibrate really well is under say... 0.5mm or less. I am really stingy about this, but for someone who isn't this isn't a big thing to worry about.

Next are the hotkeys which act more like a macbook's butterfly keyboard in terms of presses. They press well and have very little travel almost like the old iphone home buttons. This may bother some, but didn't for me. I did need to place some tape with texture to understand where my buttons were without looking.

The screen protector I didn't install and I found it really annoying to even attempt to install. Then again I've written with fountain pens for 5 years now so am very used to buttery smooth pen work.
text_fidelity_b: GAOMON PD1560 15.6 Inches 8192 Levels Pen Display with Arm Stand 1920 x 1080 HD IPS Screen Drawing Tablet with 10 Shortcut Keys

text_fidelity_a:
Nikon D3100 DSLR Camera with 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Auto Focus-S Nikkor Zoom Lens (Discontinued by Manufacturer) First, let me preface that I in NO way count myself a photog. I am just a shutter bug who has been firing frames almost non-stop since the age of 18. I learned on my dad's 'old' Nikon SLR with an f/1.2 lens. The Nikon SLRs/DSLRs I have owned are: N50, N60, N55, N80 and D50. My N50 ad N80 had the best lenses. The N60 and N55 were not as great and the D50 was a fabulous entry-level digital. The only medium format camera I own is my Holga. But hey, unlike the photographer at Portrait Innovations, at least I know 'medium format' does not refer to the number of megapixels at which I am shooting. As for my working knowledge, I had three semesters of photography in college. I can process/print both B&W and color film. (Not that that does me any good these days LOL) I can shoot completely 'manual' and I have stood among many pro photographers on the bridge at sunset, waiting for the color to be just right on Half Dome. (My Bogen tripod was way too heavy to be practical for an amateur but it gave me street credit.) So, in a nut shell, I shoot by the 'Sunny 16' rule. I know that opening my f-stop should increase my shutter speed give me a shorter depth of field; and, per the great Ansel Adams, f/8 is a proper exposure for all pictures.

That said, I hate my D3100.

I have had metering issues since I opened the box. I bought the camera so I could take 'even better' pictures of my infant son than I was getting from my D50. Ha. Joke was on me.

The contrast was BLINDING on the factory settings and every shot was over exposed. I have tried every metering option in the menu but the only changes I can achieve are under-exposure, blurred focus and missed shots. It's go high or go without.

I always lower my ISO to 100 when I'm outside because I crave rich color but it's just not there. I have tried Aperture Priority, Shutter Priority and Manual. Nothing. f/16 over my film speed on a sunny day. That's supposed to work! I have used it on many a 'less complicated' camera and achieved photos that make jaws drop. Well, there's no jaw dropping with this camera.

The metering overrides my manual choices every time. It's like I'm having a battle of wits with my camera. :( It reminds me of the days when Kodak was marketing 800-speed film as a universal, never-miss-a-shot solution to all your photo woes. Bleh. Just because there's always an image doesn't mean it's the RIGHT exposure.

I get that being an entry-level/made-for-the-masses DSLR really does mean it's a glorified point-and-shoot but it should preform at least as well as it's predecessors. Honestly, I got far more reliable results from my Canon SureShot and a roll of Kodak 100.

My expectation for a camera is that the image should be very close to perfect when the shutter closes. I know there's always room for improvement before printing but that's the art of photography. The hours I spend working on my photos after the shot should be to make them pop. Instead, my time is spent trying to rescue precious memories.

If you are considering this camera as your first DSLR because you think it will improve your skills, skip it. Invest in an equally expensive point-and-shoot that will give you all the same manual controls and preform much better in low-light situations. The D3100 does not live up to the standards of a Nikon SLR.

I gave it a second star because my son pulled mine off the counter about a year after I bought it and although the case cracked, it didn't seem to hurt the camera. Unfortunately, it impact didn't help it, either. (Yes, I was actually hopeful.)
text_fidelity_b: Nikon D3100 DSLR Camera with 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Auto Focus-S Nikkor Zoom Lens (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

Amazon Basics Laptop Desk Stand for PC and MacBook - Silver So far, I haven't found a good solution to making laptops ergonomic. Basically, you end up having to decide which matters more: your neck, or your wrists.

With this handy and sleek item, you help your neck at the expense of your wrists. Your laptop will be closer to eye level, which is the healthiest option for your neck. (Looking down often over a long length of time WILL cause neck issues.) You sacrifice your wrists, however. Wrists will not love this, as it places them at an awkward angle. Over time, it might cause some problems or exacerbate existing ones. I suppose necks are generally more important, as well as more fragile, but it's really something to consider.

As for the design, it is very nice! The aesthetic is clean and modern with a minimalist flavor. The grips on the bottom further ensure a stable base, as does the little ledge on the part where the laptop sits.

Tl:dr version: Great for your neck, not so much for your wrists; attractive

text_fidelity_a:
Canon EF-S 10-18mm f/4.5-5.6 is STM Lens, Lens Only I really bought a Canon DSLR (vs Nikon, or any of the mirrorless Cameras) for this lens. I needed a low distortion very wide lens for real estate videos and I also needed image stabilization and quiet focusing. I don't think there is any other lens from any manufacturer that satisfies all of those things except this one. (Sigma has the 10-20mm but no stabilization, lower optical quality, and more money! Tamaron - 10-24 - same story. And so on ).
GOOD: Excellent optical quality for the price. This lens is noticeably sharper and has less distortion at 10mm than my kit lens 18-135mm has at 18mm. Stabilization works very well. Focusing is very fast and silent. I don't hear it even with the built in mic when shooting video (on a Canon 70D). Extremely lightweight and fairly compact.

BAD: Maximum Aperture. This is NOT a fast lens. F/4.5 maximum is not that great and you lose it pretty quickly as you zoom in since the max aperture ranges from 4.5 - 5.6. You need to have some decent light to shoot with this lens. But given the lack of competition in super wide stabilized silent EF-S lenses (or any Canon mount lens) and the price of anything vaguely similar, I think it's a reasonable compromise.

Note: At this price, you can't really call it a knock, but it'd be nice if it came with the lens hood. You can get a clone lens hood for $10 or so.

ALSO: Canon has now updated their EOS Utility software for this lens.
text_fidelity_b: Canon EF-S 10-18mm f/4.5-5.6 is STM Lens, Lens Only

text_fidelity_a:
TP-Link Deco Mesh WiFi System(Deco M5) –Up to 5,500 sq. ft. Whole Home Coverage and 100+ Devices,WiFi Router/Extender Replacement, Anitivirus, 3-pack This review is for the TP-LInk Mesh WiFi M5 system.
—————
Amended April 28, 2020
Now that I’ve been using this for a couple weeks, I am returning to add these units HAVE NOT cured the dead spots that needed more signal strength. Yes, the WiFi signal is present in those areas of my home. However, the signal strength has not improved over what my centrally located router produced on its own. Essentially for my roughly $125, I got a couple stylish WiFi access points. What I DID NOT GET is the improved coverage promoted in the description.
—————
This IS NOT a plug it in and it works system. You need to know at minimum:
—Your current router’s IP address, the user ID for it, and the password. If you haven’t changed them from the default, you have no business installing a network anything, because you put EVERYTHING on your system at high risk for hacking. Why? The problem is that the default user ID and password are the SAME FOR ALL routers of the same brand (every brand router has a published default user id and password).
—You need to know which of several comm protocols your ISP uses.
—You need to know that IF YOU SWAP OUT YOUR ROUTER for one of the units, the others WILL NOT WORK to extend your WiFi network. For that you need to set these up as extenders, with the first being connected to your existing router.
—To set up a network of WiFi extenders, you need to know how to turn your existing router’s WiFi transmission off. Only then can you use these as extenders, satellites, or whatever you know them as.
—You are highly likely to have to update the firmware on each M5 device.
—You should set aside about two to three hours to set up a network of multiple devices.
—If you set these up as extenders, some of the default security features are switched off. You need to be sure these security features are enabled on your router instead.

I found this an unacceptably under-documented product that forces you to comb through the internet for proper setup tips. I loathe their little booklet that is “documentation” since it is a collection of single pages in multiple languages that direct you to the App Store or Google Play for the app that manages setup. That app is underpowered, has little relevant or helpful information.

I’ve been working with and installing systems from early (1990s) mainframes, Apple IIs, Macs, PCs of all flavors, and networks right up to now. Were it not for that experience, I might never have gotten this to work. Once installed, it works fine.

Recommendation: If your current router is older, you’re probably more likely to get better WiFi coverage by purchasing a newer, more current router. Try that first, and if you don't get the coverage you need, add a couple or three of these.
text_fidelity_b: TP-Link Deco Mesh WiFi System(Deco M5) –Up to 5,500 sq. ft. Whole Home Coverage and 100+ Devices,WiFi Router/Extender Replacement, Anitivirus, 3-pack

WiFi Extender Long Range Repeater 300Mbps Router Wireless Access Point Signal Amplifier Booster Complies with 802.11n/g/b with WPS Button,Extends WiFi to Smart Home & Alexa Devices Just got this today because we are having wifi accessibility issues in our upstairs guest bedroom (and every good host knows that if you don't have decent wifi in your guest room, you can expect your guests to leave you a holy mess, in retaliation).

Couldn't believe how easy this is to set up, though! I'm pretty tech-savvy, anyhow (after 2 years of various tech-related military schools). Not that I needed to be! The included instructions are incredibly clear and easy to follow. On the contrary, the last AP/repeater I bought merely schooled me in when it's acceptable to take a hammer to one of these things. (FYI: it's right after you've tried, unsuccessfully, for an hour to get it to connect to your wifi). So I really appreciated how simple and fast this is to set up.

How fast, exactly? It literally took like 2 minutes to set up...and only THAT long because I had to go all the way into the other room and log into my laptop to complete the instructions.

Just a head's up, for the less-tech savvy:

This is NOT a wifi signal amplifier, as such. You WILL be creating a NEW wireless access point (aka wifi log-on)...even if you install this in "repeater" mode--vs. the wired-to-wireless AP (access point) mode.

So, for example, instead of logging into whatever your network is called, when you need to use the wifi that this repeats for you, you'll be logging into a new connection. They call it, by default, "My Repeater" (I assume that is so you'll never forget who actually owns it), but you can rename it to anything you want (mine is henceforth known as Fluffy Gigglebuns). You'll still use the same password as you use for your main connection, though...and therein lies the genius of it. You can make your guests feel special (or, in my case, humiliated) by personalizing the repeater network name, but the password will be the same as it is for whatever network AP you are having it repeat.

Lastly, this does offer an extra feature I think is worth mentioning:

You can also use this as a wireless adapter to connect a multimedia or other tech device that requires or ONLY allows internet connectivity via an ethernet (aka wired) connection.

So if you have something like an older roku, or game console, etc. that can only connect to the internet via an ethernet cable, you can apparently use THIS device to quickly convert it to use your wifi connection.
text_fidelity_b: WiFi Extender Long Range Repeater 300Mbps Router Wireless Access Point Signal Amplifier Booster Complies with 802.11n/g/b with WPS Button,Extends WiFi to Smart Home & Alexa Devices

I only received my Targus backpack yesterday, but from the looks of it I am pretty darn sure this backpack will last a long, long time. I've used MANY backpacks in the past carrying books, laptops and supplies during the time it took to earn two separate college degrees, and at my previous job of 17 years. I had to carry tools, manuals, laptops and assorted parts to calibrate monitoring equipment around my state. I was rough on the backpacks and some wore out.

I really wish I had had a backpack like this one. It's very well constructed out of strong materials, has a plethora of pockets and places to organize your stuff, and though I don't have a 17" notebook as of yet, it appears to be deep and wide and should easily fit one. There are even slots for file folders and inside zipper pouches. There are pockets on the inside and pockets on the outside. The bottom inside has a foam rubber "shock pad" that neatly folds down flat on the bottom of the backpack and is about 1/2" thick. Plus the bottom is covered in a waterproof rubbery material that should definitely help keep water from seeping up into the bag. That happened to me several times on my job with my other backpacks and it was really frustrating. It's very easy to set your backpack down on the ground not realizing the area is wet.

The shoulder straps are padded and adjustable, and it has a waist strap for extra stability. Even if you didn't use this backpack to tote your 17" marvel of technology around, it would serve well as a camper/hiker backpack. I can't wait to start using it. If something should go wrong or tear up, I will most definitely update this review telling about it, but for now I can find no fault whatsoever with it.

USB Power Strip Tower, BESFAN Surge Protector with 12 Outlets and 5 USB Ports, 10ft Extension Cord USB (Desktop Smart Charging Station) for Home, Dorm and Office As most of us know – if we have electronics (laptops, iPads, phones) – we need a surge protector.

And, since about 2003 – I’ve had TONS of them. Even ones that protected the landline cord (do we even have landlines anymore). I’ve had wide/flat, narrow/flat, and just ones that mounted to a wall.

I’ve had ones that didn’t have enough outlets either, or the outlets were spaced just “so” that I couldn’t plug up adapter type plugs (phones, etc). And, ones that the wall cord was so short they didn’t help out much in certain areas.

This one?

WOW! Game changer!

Not only the shape – I would never have thought of a tower design. But, it does save room. I have mine under my desk and with my old flat one – I ended up turning it off countless times. Not this one though. Outlets? 12 outlets which comes in handy, along with five (5) USB ports.

This is a LONG wall cord so plugging it into outlets further/farther away than where you need it is not a huge problem. Unless the outlet is across the room.

The outlets on this unit are spaced and sectioned for big or small plugs. And, the USB ports are a huge bonus! Some devices don’t come with a wall adapter and either you spend money on one, or you have to hook it up to your computer. This? That eliminates that situation.

I can’t attest to others’ and their phones – this charges my phone in the same amount of time as the wall adapter to the USB cord would. So, not much difference there.

Other than the cool stuff, this functions just like other surge protectors. No issues so far. It’s fairly sturdy and I’m definitely glad I got this! I’m definitely sold on this design and I plan to upgrade my household with them as I can.

I definitely wouldn’t hesitate to recommend this. Would make a great “house-warming” gift.

Canon PowerShot A1400 16.0 MP Digital Camera with 5x Digital Image Stabilized Zoom 28mm Wide-Angle Lens and 720p HD Video Recording (Black) (OLD MODEL) These cameras are amazing. Get a 32GB chip, put CHDK on it and you can do awesome stuff with this camera. I bought two for my family's trip to Alaska, and we snapped thousands of photos. Very good quality, fair low light performance, controls are easy enough. We spent a fair bit of time learning the controls so we'd be fluent with them.

Here's a neat trick: You can use these cameras as low power microscopes. Put the Macro setting on, take a photo as near ask the thing will focus, which is pretty close, then hit 'Play' and use the zoom lever on the shutter release to zoom in and get a microscope view of what you took the photo of.

Also, with CHDK on the SD card, you have a built in intervelometer for taking time lapse sequences.

Another fun thing to do is to take night time photos of the sky using the long exposure setting. With the 10 second setting and the ISO turned up you can capture images of stars or northern lights in the night sky. Fantastic for a $60 camera.

After break-in, these MEE buds were sounding like something that cost 4-5 times as much with a nice, even frequency response that favors bass only slightly. I find them comparable to $60-$80 Sennheisers, my previous favorites (which superseded Sony and Koss buds that I also liked). These MEE buds came with 3 sets (S, M, and L) of your typical soft rubber earpieces as well as 2 sets of the interesting multi-tiered earpieces shown in the photos and a pretty standard cloth case. Between the various earpiece options, it's unlikely anyone will have an issue finding a good fit.

The cord is about 1 m long, which suits my purposes. I like the over-the-ear wire bits, too, as they prevent tugs on the cord from dislodging them. They might be awkward with some kinds of glasses, but my straight-earpiece sunglasses fit over them fine. They can be bent to hang down more like normal earbuds if desired, though.

I'll be checking out more MEE products now, seeing what a great value these were. I still favor AKG and Beyerdynamic at the high end, but for my biking/hiking/running/workout listening needs, I'll probably be coming back to MEE.

This bluetooth receiver, in ear buds or headphones is the best I own or have purchased.  I use them mostly for watching TV, silently in my home living room, early and late.  The are kind of tight fitting on my ears, , but do have soft ear pads.  Each side adjusts an extra inch of fit size and this is adequate for my big round head.  I would recommend them to be folded when they are at their smallest size, as it is kinda flimsy when full opened up.  The controls are on the bottom of the left side; power on/phone button, aux input jack, charge micro usb port, and forward/back/play/pause slide button.  I like them and feel the price with delivery is a pretty good deal.  They sound pretty good when you are listening to Bluetooth, a signal that is not too good for audio fidelity quality, so don't expect plug in quality as a bluetooth receiver.  This headphone can be plugged in and used as a regular cabled set of headphones also.  The bluetooth has the best range of any bluetooth receiver I own.  To hear what they really can sound like, plug them in to the jack and listen to a CD or another high fidelity source, besides MP3, Bluetooth or "Radio" satellite, all sources which are notorious for poor fidelity,  as these are not great HiFi sound signals.  Sound has gone way down hill with these formats for electronics for the masses.  I don't listen to Bluetooth much or these other low fidelity formats with the music I like and if I did, I would prefer to use these headphones, rather than ear buds of similar price.  Of course, much more expensive products can be purchased, but I won't, as I have in the past and they are not worth the investment of my money.

text_fidelity_a:
RackPath 1U 19 Inch Plastic Server Rack Mount Cable Management Duct Raceway with Panel Cover For the record, I prefer the European-version of the Rittal Cable Management Panels (CMPs) that are just a metal plate with easy to slide into metal arms. But I've never seen them in the States, however, I have seen some sort of similar, but with plastic arms.

This style is much more common in the States, but trying this has helped me to appreciate it a little bit more. I guess I normally don't like them because in "public" telecom rooms (by public, I mean multiple people working on/in them), these type are always so full and messy that no one ever puts the fronts on correctly. In my private telecom cabinet, of course I keep it looking nice. The front closure can maneuver down or up as if on a hinge and snaps into place well. I see now, how routing through the different "fingers" can work very well if you're being careful and care about looks and quality of routing. I have CatX cables going between the fingers, but have some DACs going to the side and in to accommodate a more generous bend radius.

What really works nicely in my case (although I think, ideally you have a wide enough cabinet with enough CMPs that you don't have to do this) is that I can take the cables through the holes in the back plate, circle and secure them, and then come back in the back plate, which mitigates patch cables that are longer than necessary. I honestly can't remember if the big brands have those holes in the base plate.

In a home situation, I'm not going to have problems with the fingers bending and the cover no longer fitting on because I take care of my stuff.

Oh, worth noting is that this does not seem to be as deep as the ones you see in data centers by the big brands. They may have done that on purpose, figuring a lot of homeowners don't have 100cm deep racks (or, if they do, they didn't allow for enough space in the front).

Overall, this is very good for me. I'm not sure if they're making these for the homeowner/power user market, or trying to break into the data center world, but it certainly works for the former.
text_fidelity_b: RackPath 1U 19 Inch Plastic Server Rack Mount Cable Management Duct Raceway with Panel Cover

text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR WiFi Mesh Range Extender EX6400 - Coverage up to 2100 sq.ft. and 35 devices with AC1900 Dual Band Wireless Signal Booster & Repeater (up to 1900Mbps speed), plus Mesh Smart Roaming Works well if you can figure it out

I bought a Netgear EX6250 in a brick-and-mortar store about four months ago and my experience with it has been good overall...though not without its complications. Past experience with late-model Netgear products can be helpful in getting this unit set up and operating as the process is not always straightforward. It took me (who has a lot of experience with Netgear products and home networking in general) rather a few tries to get onto the right track in the Nighthawk app to set the thing up - you can run into roadblocks due to aspects of the Nighthawk app's design being less than intuitive (I know I did). I can't remember specifics now...so you know what I'm going to do? Out of lovingfriendliness for my fellow Amazon customers, I'm going to reset the extender to factory settings and set it back up, taking notes along the way, so that I can relate my experience more clearly and in greater detail.

Okay, so:

First you want to jump online and download the Netgear Nighthawk app to your phone. I don’t know if this unit can be set up without it.

Next, plug the extender into power - somewhere where it’s in range of your router. After you first plug the unit in, or after resetting it using the little recessed paperclip button on the side, the power LED will glow orange for rather a long time - two to three minutes in my experience - before finally turning green. Green means “go” - but orange doesn’t. So you just have to wait until that light turns green in order to be able to proceed with the setup process. Good opportunity to focus on the breath. And the fact that patience is a virtue.

Once the power indicator turns green, launch the Nighthawk app and check the little circle confirming that you accept Netgear’s terms and conditions and that you’ve read their privacy policy…even though you probably haven’t. Then tap “I Agree”.

On an iPhone, at least, the next screen says that iOS requires that you enable local network access in order to be able to set up your extender (which at this point the Nighthawk app is calling a “router” because it doesn’t yet know any better - you haven’t yet told it what you want to set up). Obviously, since you want to set up your extender, you’re going to okay that local network access. Tap “Continue” and your phone will ask you if you want to allow the app to find and connect to devices on your local network. Tap “OK”.

The next screen asks you to allow push notifications. This one’s up to you. I think I’ve always allowed them and I haven’t seen one yet, let alone been annoyed by excessive/unwanted notifications that are, in the end, just trying to sell me crap or otherwise waste my time.

The next screen tells you Netgear needs access to your device’s location services to automatically connect to your wifi network. I always allow this.

Next you’re told you have to create a new Netgear account or log into an existing one. Do that.

Then you’ll be asked if you want to enable Face ID and you’ll also be asked…something else I forget because I just blazed past it, momentarily forgetting that I was writing this detailed description of the process. But…y’know. You can read (because you’re reading this), so…tap the things on your screen that accord with your wishes. :)

At last we come to a screen that says, “Let’s set up your Nighthawk”, and tells you what to do if the unit’s been set up before. I don’t think I’ve ever had any luck using the “been set up before” option, so I always reset the extender to factory settings (by pressing and holding the paperclip/pen-point button on the side of the unit until the power light blinks orange) when I have a problem with the connection (which I seldom do, and when I do it’s usually because the power’s blinked or something else explicit has happened to make me need to set the extender up again). If this is your first time setting it up, tap “Set up a Nighthawk”. Even though I don’t think this extender is technically a Nighthawk. Doesn’t matter - you can still set it up with this app.

Next you’re shown a rundown of what’s going to happen. Read that as you’re inclined, then tap “Get Started!”.

On the product selection screen that comes up next, tap “Range Extender”.

The app tells you where to plug in your extender. Follow its instructions and tap “Next”.

The next screen just tells you to actually plug it in now, and wait (…and wait…and wait…) for a solid (green) power LED. Do that, and when you’ve got the solid green power light, tap “Next”.

On the next screen, the app will ask you to let it join your extender’s network. Tap “OK”, and wait while your phone connects to your extender. When it does, the screen will change to display “Great, we found your extender”. Tap “Next”.

Tap “Next” on the next screen as well.

Now your phone will look for your router’s network (which is your pre-existing wifi network, the one you want to extend). I think what it’s doing now is acting as a liaison between your router and the extender - introducing them to one another, as it were. Because what happens next is that your extender looks for and - ideally - connects to your wifi network. (When you’re asked to allow…something…to join your network, tap “Join”.)

And if all has gone well, that’s pretty much it. You’ll see a screen that says you’re up and running, and…there it is: you’re up and running!

Obviously, all of that is how things are *supposed* to go. If they go otherwise…you’ll probably need to be able to apply a searing laser beam of logic to the process and figure out how to make it work (that’s been my personal approach and, lucky for me, it’s always worked so far), or else to contact the dread Netgear Support People. I hope for your sake the laser beam works.

Good luck and enjoy!
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR WiFi Mesh Range Extender EX6400 - Coverage up to 2100 sq.ft. and 35 devices with AC1900 Dual Band Wireless Signal Booster & Repeater (up to 1900Mbps speed), plus Mesh Smart Roaming

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech MX Keys Mini Minimalist Wireless Illuminated Keyboard, Compact, Bluetooth, Backlit, USB-C, Compatible with Apple macOS, iOS, Windows, Linux, Android, Metal Build - Graphite I’ve been using the Logitech MX Keys Mini for about two weeks now. I like it, but I don’t love it. The keyboard won’t replace my current favored mechanical keyboard, I love linear switches too much, but it has some uses.

The typing experience is decent. The keyboard is at a fixed angle, it cannot be adjusted. The bottom of the keyboard does have rubber “feet” so that it doesn’t slide around. No movement on my desk mat or plain desktop. The keys have what Logitech calls a “spherical dish” which looks like a little cup on the top of each key. My fingers naturally settle in the indentation but it’s not something I notice when typing.

The keyboard isn’t silent, but it’s much, much quieter than a mechanical keyboard. There’s a little tactile feedback, so I do feel the keypresses, which I like.

The form factor of the keyboard is, well, mini. The size makes it a good solution if you don’t have a lot of space on your desk or want to take it on the go. Logitech made some sacrifices with keys, but did keep the arrow keys. Whew. If you need a numpad, this isn’t the keyboard for you.

I really wish the backlighting could be controlled via the keyboard. The brightness can be adjusted, but that’s it. Otherwise, the keyboard is “smart” enough to know when you are typing and illuminate, but when your hands aren’t on it, or you stop typing for a few seconds, the backlighting turns off. When I’m using my computer in the dark, reading an article or watching something, it’s really annoying to have the backlighting flicker in and out.

The backlighting and other customization options are set in Logi Options, Logitech’s software. I already use Logi Options for my MX Master 3 mouse, but try as I might, I could not get the software to recognize the keyboard. I have to use High Sierra for a program I rely on, and after going through a bunch of suggested troubleshooting, I think that’s why. So if you’re like me and using an older version of macOS, you might have trouble getting the keyboard recognized by Logi Options. Because of this, I can’t use Flow, either.

The MX Keys Mini can connect with up to 3 devices at once, the first three function keys allow quick switching between devices. I tried to pair my MacBookPro and Note20 Ultra to test this, and was able to easily pair both and switch. The keyboard ONLY connects to devices via Bluetooth or the Logi Bolt USB Receiver (which isn’t included). A USB-A to USB-C cable is included for charging only. Because I can’t get Logi Options to recognize the keyboard, I can’t check battery life and know when it needs to be charged.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech MX Keys Mini Minimalist Wireless Illuminated Keyboard, Compact, Bluetooth, Backlit, USB-C, Compatible with Apple macOS, iOS, Windows, Linux, Android, Metal Build - Graphite

I could care less about any sports channel or 90% of everything else. It is my opinion that we should be able to choose extra channels separately after we hook up with basic cable. You'll also notice that BH charges extra for a special HD tier. Sure it's only $6 a month, but geez, look how much markup there is. Anyways, you get the idea. I don't have any issues with BH. They've served me well for a few years. But I need more of what I want. Not what BH thinks I want.

So, I dropped down to basic cable and purchased a Roku HD unit. Set-up was a snap. I used HDMI for the TV and stream with a N router.

OMFG! This thing is amazing! In short, it streams unlimited Netflix offerings to your TV. The cheapest Netflix subscription ($9) is all you need. Plus it streams Amazon Video On Demand, and a bunch of internet channels. You can stream wirelessly or hard wire with an ethernet cable.

Can you tell I'm excited? Anytime I can boost my entertainment for less dollars is always a good day. The Roku will pay for itself in 2 months after switching to basic. And its HD!

Sigh...I must go.

I've been watching the original Dr. Who from the 60's.
text_fidelity_b: Roku N1100 HD Media Player (Old Model)

Based on the reviews it seemed like it would do the job and it seemed simple which is all we needed.

The connections are very simple and its a good looking speaker. Ideal for placing in that little space beneath a monitor in front of the stand. The headphone jack and manual volume dial is also a nice touch.

So everything up to the point of unboxing and connecting was great. Then we turned on the sound. It is tinny, there was no bass or even midrange body, and there was tons of distortion even at a modest volume. The best way I could characterize it is an old AM clock radio with a single speaker from the 70s. There wasn't anyway I could push decent volume out of these speakers and I tried every combination of source and speaker volume I could figure. If I was trying to use this on a laptop I wouldn't even bother. Better off with a cheap pair of computer speakers from Walmart.

Giving it two stars really because it does work, it had nice features, and it plays sound for very little money. But if you want better sound than what comes out of a cheap radio, spend a little more and get a lot more out of it. I can't imagine this speaker being useful in any way.

text_fidelity_a:
Plantronics 211856-99 Backbeat Fit 3100 True Wireless Earbuds, Sweatproof and Waterproof In Ear Workout Headphones, Grey There are "true wireless" earbuds on Amazon for half of this price, but I have tried several of them and they all suffer from poor-to-mediocre sound quality as well as poor battery life. These Plantronics earbuds cost more, but they have great sound quality as well as great battery life. I hear a good amount of bass as well as good clarity in the higher frequencies. My favorite music sounds muddy on cheaper wireless earbuds, but sounds great on these. 5 hour battery life per charge is almost double what the cheap earbuds give me. The ear hooks look clunky, but they are very comfortable and never fall off when I'm jogging or working out.

As with all "true wireless" earbuds, you have to control them with a series of short and long taps on the sides of the earbuds (to change volume, skip around in your music, answer phone calls, etc). If you have a hard time remembering all those commands (as I do), you can always pull out your phone and do the same thing from there.

If you cannot afford "true wireless" earbuds at this price level, my advice is to forget the "true wireless" design and look at Bluetooth earbuds that have a wire connecting the two sides. That style is slightly uglier than "true wireless" but has much better battery life and sound quality for similar price levels and there are pretty good products for much cheaper prices than the "true wireless" design.

I see some review complaints about connectivity and charging problems. My earbuds have worked perfectly with no dropouts, etc. As with any electronic gadget, there is always the possibility of a manufacturing flaw. I would definitely return a product that did not work flawlessly.

Note that this particular Plantronics model is not noise-cancelling or noise-isolating. You will hear some background noise, which is safer if you use them when walking or working in a busy environment. Plantronics does sell noise cancelling earbuds that you could choose instead if that feature is useful and important to you.
text_fidelity_b: Plantronics 211856-99 Backbeat Fit 3100 True Wireless Earbuds, Sweatproof and Waterproof In Ear Workout Headphones, Grey

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm X-E2 16.3 MP Mirrorless Digital Camera with 3.0-Inch LCD - Body Only (Silver) I've been thinking about upgrading from my Canon 50d for awhile now. I thought I wanted a full frame camera, but I could never justify spending that kind of money on a hobby. One of the main reasons was that I had sort of got out of the habit of shooting as much as I used. Part of the reason was that it always seemed like such a pain to lug around the camera. There were always times I wish I had a camera, but didn't.

This camera solves a lot of that for me. Take the lens off the body and the thing literally fits in your pocket. Leave it on and it fits nicely in my car's center console. It feels nice in my hands, although I bought the metal thumb grip at the same time as the camera and must admit that does help quite a bit.

Compared to my 50d (which is a little long in the tooth) the image quality is superior. The color reproduction in particular seemed to be good. It also seemed to perform better at higher ISOs than my 50d does. Really, the only area where the 50d still out-performs the XE-2 is how fast the autofocus works. The XE-2 is good, but my 50d is still a touch better. Maybe a firmware update will improve this.

Despite using a Canon products for almost a decade, I found I really like the controls on this camera. I found it really easy and intuitive to change the shutter speed and aperature. ISO and most of the other frequently used settings are easily reached by hitting the Q button. The layout could be tweaked a little, but overall it's pretty good.

I've never had a camera with wifi, but it's a feature that's gotten more use than I thought it would. Being able to transmit pictures to Facebook, Twitter, or whatever is really simple once you upload the photo from the camera using Fuji's app. I don't post a lot of pictures online, but that may change a little bit now that it is a lot simpler.

The build quality is really good and the included kit lens is really nice. The screen is sharp and the EVF is clear. Like I mentioned before, the size of the frame is nice and compact and is much easier to take along wherever you go.

Is this a replacement for a full frame DSLR? No. Is it a good alternative for a crop sensor DSLR? In my opinion, absolutely. First, the price and performance makes it very competitive. Second, the size is going to be tough to beat. Finally, for me at least, it is a camera I am more likely to use more and take with me more places. As other's have mentioned about this camera though, if you like putting everything on automatic or different shooting modes (sports, portrait, landscape, etc) then this camera is probably not for you. If you are interested in learning how to shoot without those crutches, this camera would be a great place to start.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm X-E2 16.3 MP Mirrorless Digital Camera with 3.0-Inch LCD - Body Only (Silver)
